g.text: Why joins are hard on streams — no completion, and a buffer
5 true matches · 1 on time · 2 after a retraction · 2 never emitted
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · "a" = clicks, "b" = impressions · join window 60s
A BATCH JOIN COMPLETES; A STREAM-STREAM JOIN DOES NOT
the bound is what gives the query a meaning at all
batch: 5 clicks x 4 impressions
20 candidate pairs, all testable, then done
stream: the same two inputs
either side may still produce a match — forever
so the join needs a TIME BOUND
match rows whose event times are within 60s of each other
within that bound, truly matching pairs
Without the bound the join would have to retain every row of both sides forever, in case a match arrives.
So the time bound is not an optimisation — it is what makes the state finite AND the semantics defined.
Step 1/4 — two unbounded inputs have no moment at which the join is done
A batch join over these inputs tests 20 pairs and finishes. The streaming version never finishes on its own, so a time bound is mandatory — and
with a 60s bound there are exactly 5 true matches here: 0-7, 1-7, 3-2, 4-5, 4-6. Everything that follows is about which of those 5 actually get
emitted.
Why joins are hard on streams — no completion, and a buffer
5 true matches · 1 on time · 2 after a retraction · 2 never emitted
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · "a" = clicks, "b" = impressions · join window 60s
WHAT IS HELD IN JOIN STATE, EVENT BY EVENT
rows still within 60s of the join's watermark, so a match could still arrive for them
id 0
id 1
id 2
id 3
id 4
id 5
id 6
id 7
id 8
The buffer peaks at 5 rows on this 9-row stream, and it is bounded only because the join window is.
Each buffered row is waiting for a counterpart that may never come. A join's state is therefore proportional to arrival rate times the join
window.
Step 2/4 — the join must BUFFER one side while waiting for the other
Rows cannot be matched and discarded immediately — each one waits for a counterpart. The buffer peaks at 5 rows here, and the only reason it peaks
at all rather than growing is the 60s window. That makes join state (arrival rate × join window), which is the sizing formula to carry away.
Why joins are hard on streams — no completion, and a buffer
5 true matches · 1 on time · 2 after a retraction · 2 never emitted
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · "a" = clicks, "b" = impressions · join window 60s
WHEN EACH CLICK'S RESULT MAY BE EMITTED
the join claims min(left, right) — ch03's rule, with two inputs by construction
click id 0 (et 12:00:01)
after event 5, when the minimum watermark passes 12:01:01
click id 1 (et 12:00:03)
after event 5, when the minimum watermark passes 12:01:03
click id 3 (et 12:02:10)
after event 8, when the minimum watermark passes 12:03:10
click id 4 (et 12:04:05)
NEVER — the join watermark never passes 12:05:05
click id 8 (et 12:09:00)
NEVER — the join watermark never passes 12:10:00
2 of the 5 clicks never emits at all, because the MINIMUM watermark never reaches its join bound.
Those 2 rows hold 2 of the 5 true matches. They are in the state, matched, and never published.
Step 3/4 — and the watermark is what ends the wait
This is where a stream-stream join stops resembling a batch join. 3 of the 5 clicks reach an emission point; 2 never do, because the join's
watermark is the minimum over both inputs and it stalls below their bound. 2 of the 5 true matches are computed, held in state, and never
published.
Why joins are hard on streams — no completion, and a buffer
5 true matches · 1 on time · 2 after a retraction · 2 never emitted
seed: tools/stream_seed.js · "a" = clicks, "b" = impressions · join window 60s
TWO JOINS, TWO BOUNDING MECHANISMS
the same data, two join kinds, very different behaviour
stream JOIN stream
bounded by TIME — a window, plus both watermarks
stream JOIN table
bounded by the TABLE — one lookup per row, finite per key
here, as a windowed join
5 matches exist · 1 emitted on time · 2 never emitted
here, as a temporal join
5 rows enriched immediately, 2 with no table version yet
Mistaking one for the other is the common streaming-join bug: windowing a lookup adds a wait that the data never needed.
Read the right-hand input: if it is a slowly-changing dimension, it is a table and wants a temporal join, however it arrived.
Step 4/4 — so the input type picks the join type
The decision is about what is being joined, not how the data got there. Two streams need a time bound and inherit all of the above — 1 of 5
matches on time here. A stream against a table is a lookup, bounded per key, and all 5 rows are enriched at once. The bug is windowing the second
case.
